title: OSINT Tooling, Entity Graphs, and Defensible Threat-Intel Reporting
intro: OSINT tooling is the set of programs, frameworks, and report formats that let an analyst collect public information at scale, connect it into a coherent picture, and hand it to decision makers in a form they can trust. This lesson explains what each tool category is for, how link analysis and structured sharing work, how to stay passive and lawful while automating, and how to write a report whose claims, confidence, and limits are all explicit.

sections.heading: Tool categories and when to use each
sections.content:
OSINT tooling is not one product. It is a family of programs that collect, correlate, and organize public information faster than manual browsing. Each category answers a different question, and picking the category before picking the tool prevents the most common beginner error: launching a heavy automated scan when one quiet, targeted lookup would have answered the question without anyone noticing.

| Category | Example | What it does | Typical defensive use | Main risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Link analysis / aggregator | Maltego | Builds a graph of entities; transforms call many data sources and return related entities | Mapping the infrastructure and personas behind a phishing campaign | A tidy graph looks authoritative even when edges are weak |
| Automated reconnaissance | SpiderFoot | Runs many modules against a target (domain, IP, email, name) and stores correlated results | Footprinting your own organization or a suspicious domain | Noisy active modules and high false-positive volume |
| Scriptable recon framework | Recon-ng | Modular command-line framework with a workspace database and a key store | Repeatable, documented recon pipelines | Module quality varies; needs API keys |
| Harvester | theHarvester | Collects emails, subdomains, hosts, and names from search engines, certificate transparency, and APIs | Seeing your own domain footprint the way an attacker sees it | Stale sources; brute-force and DNS modules are active |
| Directory | The OSINT Framework | A browsable tree of tools and resources organized by task | Finding which resource covers a niche question | It is a map, not a tool; links go stale |

**How to choose.** Start from the question, not the tool. 'What does the public internet reveal about my own domain?' points to a harvester run against passive sources, followed by a passive-only SpiderFoot scan for correlation. 'How is this phishing domain connected to the other twelve we saw?' points to link analysis. 'I need the same recon repeated every week and logged' points to Recon-ng with a saved workspace. 'I do not know where to look for information about a shipping registry' points to the OSINT Framework directory, which only tells you where to go.

**What is important to know.** Tools are collectors, not analysts. They return candidates, and every candidate still needs a source, a timestamp, and a judgment. Versions and module lists change often, so read the current documentation before relying on a module, and record the version in your notes.

**What is important to ask.** What exact question am I answering? What is the least intrusive source that can answer it? Will this module touch the target's systems, or only third-party data? What will I do with the output, and who needs it?

**Pitfall: tool over-reliance.** An analyst who only trusts what a tool printed cannot explain why a result is true. Treat tool output as a lead list and verify the important items by a second independent source. For single-indicator reputation and context lookups (IP, domain, hash), use the enrichment tools lesson; this lesson is about the wider workflow around those lookups.

sections.heading: Link analysis and entity graphs
sections.content:
Link analysis represents an investigation as a graph. **Entities** are the nodes: domains, IP addresses, email addresses, people or aliases, organizations, certificates, ASNs, social accounts, file hashes. **Edges** are the relationships between them: resolves-to, registered-by, hosted-on, issued-to, follows, mentions. A good graph records for every edge where the relationship came from and when it was observed.

A **transform** is a function that takes one entity and returns related entities. A domain goes in; the IPs it resolved to, its registrant contact, its nameservers, and its certificates come out. A **pivot** is the analyst's decision to follow one of those edges to a new entity and ask the next question. Maltego popularized this vocabulary, but the idea is tool-independent: you can build the same graph in a notebook or on a whiteboard.

**Reading a Maltego-style graph.** Look first at structure, not at pretty icons. Clusters of nodes tightly connected to each other suggest a shared operator or shared template. A **bridge node** that connects two clusters is the most interesting object in the graph, because it is the thing that might prove one actor runs both. A **hub** with hundreds of edges is usually not a discovery; it is typically shared hosting, a CDN, or a registrar default.

Not every edge is equally strong evidence:

| Shared attribute | Strength as a link | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Same non-privacy registrant email | Strong | Unique to a person or team unless the data was forged |
| Same analytics or tracking ID in page source | Strong | Tied to one account, rarely shared |
| Same unusual TLS certificate or key | Strong | Reuse is a deliberate or lazy operator choice |
| Same favicon hash or page template | Moderate | Kits are sold and copied |
| Same nameserver pair | Moderate to weak | Common among customers of one provider |
| Same IP on shared hosting | Weak | Thousands of unrelated sites live there |
| Same registrar or TLD | Very weak | Millions of customers |

**What is important to ask.** Is this edge unique to one operator, or common to many? Is the data current or historical (a passive DNS record from three years ago may belong to the previous owner of the IP)? Could an adversary have planted this link deliberately?

**Scenario.** Twelve lookalike domains appear to connect through one IP. The graph looks like a single operation. The IP turns out to be a budget host with thousands of tenants, so the link is weak. The analyst pivots on the registrant email of three domains and the analytics ID of five, and the case now rests on two strong, independent edges. A graph is a set of hypotheses to test, never a finding by itself.

sections.heading: Automating responsibly: limits, keys, terms, and noise
sections.content:
Automation multiplies both speed and mistakes. Four disciplines keep it safe.

**Rate limits.** Every API and website has a request budget. Exceeding it gets your key suspended, your IP blocked, and sometimes your organization flagged. Throttle tools, cache results so you never ask the same question twice, and prefer bulk endpoints to thousands of single calls.

**API keys.** Keys are credentials. Store them in the tool's key store or a secrets manager, never in scripts, notebooks, tickets, or screenshots. Use one key per project or per analyst so usage is traceable, apply the lowest privilege the service offers, and rotate when someone leaves. A leaked OSINT key can be abused in your name.

**Terms of service.** Many sites forbid automated scraping, fake accounts, or bulk collection even when the data is publicly visible. 'Public' describes visibility, not permission. Read the terms, use official APIs where they exist, and document the legal basis for anything borderline. Work that violates terms can taint the evidence and expose the organization.

**Passive versus active.** This is the most important distinction in the whole workflow.

| Passive (target is not touched) | Active (target's systems see you) |
|---|---|
| Search engines and cached or archived pages | Visiting the suspect site from your corporate network |
| Certificate transparency logs | Port or service scanning of the target |
| Passive DNS and historical WHOIS or RDAP | DNS brute-force against the target's nameservers |
| Third-party URL-scan snapshots and breach notification services | Probing login or password-reset forms to test if an email exists |
| Public code repositories and paste sites | Sending email to the target or opening tracking links |

**Why noise matters.** An adversary running a phishing site reads its access logs. A burst of requests from your corporate address range, a scanner user agent, or a lookup of the exact URL from a security vendor's netblock tells them they are being investigated. They rotate infrastructure, wipe the kit, or serve a clean decoy page, and your evidence disappears. Active touching of third-party systems may also be unlawful without authorization.

**Working rule.** Passive first. Capture the page through a third-party snapshot or an isolated, non-attributable environment before any direct visit, and only when the case needs it. Disable default-on active modules in SpiderFoot and theHarvester, explicitly choose each module, log which modules ran, and scan only assets you own or are authorized to test.

sections.heading: Managing and sharing findings: MISP, STIX, TAXII, and IOCs
sections.content:
Findings that live in one analyst's notes die when the analyst leaves. Structured threat intelligence gives findings a durable, machine-readable home.

**MISP** is an open-source threat intelligence platform. The unit is an **event** (an incident, campaign, or investigation) containing **attributes** (typed values such as domain, ip-dst, email-src, url, sha256). Related attributes can be grouped as **objects** (for example, a file with its name, hash, and size). **Tags** carry classification such as TLP marking, **galaxies** map to ATT&CK techniques or named threat actors, and a **to_ids** flag says whether an attribute is suitable for automated detection. MISP automatically correlates a new value against everything already stored, so an indicator you found today can light up an event from last year. **Warninglists** flag values that are known benign (large cloud providers, public DNS resolvers) so they do not become false-positive IOCs. Distribution settings control who may see an event.

**STIX and TAXII.** STIX 2.1 is a JSON language for describing intelligence: objects such as indicator, threat-actor, campaign, infrastructure, malware, identity, observed-data, and report, joined by relationship objects. An indicator carries a pattern, for example [domain-name:value = 'acme-payrol1-portal.example'], plus validity dates. TAXII 2.1 is the HTTPS transport: servers expose collections, and clients fetch or push STIX bundles. The short version is that STIX is the what, and TAXII is the how.

**From OSINT to IOC.** Turn findings into detections deliberately:

| OSINT finding | IOC form | Detection use | Expected lifetime |
|---|---|---|---|
| Newly registered lookalike domain | Domain | Block at DNS and proxy; hunt in resolver logs | Days to weeks |
| Phishing sender address | Email address | Mail gateway rule; search delivered mail | Days |
| Hosting IP unique to the actor | IP address | Firewall and flow hunting, with warninglist check | Days to weeks |
| Reused kit page template or tracking ID | Content pattern | Web proxy and URL-scan hunting | Weeks to months |
| Leaked employee email list | Affected-account list | Targeted awareness, MFA review, mail monitoring | Until reviewed |

Domains, IPs, and hashes are the cheapest for an adversary to change; kit patterns and behaviors cost them more. Every IOC should carry context: source, first and last seen, confidence, TLP marking, and an expiry date. An unexpiring, unsourced indicator becomes a false-positive generator.

**What is important to ask.** Is this indicator specific, or shared infrastructure? Who may receive it under its TLP marking? Does it contain personal data that must be stripped before sharing? For how indicators are produced, scored, and operationalized, see the threat-intel lesson; for per-indicator lookups, see the enrichment tools lesson.

sections.heading: Analytic rigor: hypotheses, confidence language, source rating, bias
sections.content:
Tools produce data. Rigor turns data into a judgment you can defend.

**Analysis of Competing Hypotheses (ACH).** Developed for intelligence analysis, ACH forces you to compare explanations rather than collect support for your favorite. Steps: list all plausible hypotheses, list the evidence, mark each piece of evidence as consistent, inconsistent, or neutral against each hypothesis, then focus on **diagnosticity**. Evidence consistent with every hypothesis (such as 'the domain was registered recently') proves nothing between them. The hypothesis with the fewest inconsistencies survives, and you try to disprove rather than confirm.

| Evidence | H1: Criminal credential-phishing crew | H2: Mass commodity kit campaign | H3: Authorized internal simulation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Domain registered 6 days ago | Consistent | Consistent | Consistent |
| Page lists our company name and HR branding | Consistent | Inconsistent | Consistent |
| Persona profile created 3 weeks ago | Consistent | Neutral | Inconsistent |
| No simulation ticket with the awareness team | Consistent | Consistent | Inconsistent |

The first row has no diagnostic value. The remaining rows separate H1 from H2 and H3.

**Confidence language.** Separate two ideas. **Likelihood** is how probable the event is. **Confidence** is how solid the evidence base behind that judgment is. Standard words of estimative probability keep readers aligned:

| Term | Approximate probability |
|---|---|
| Almost no chance | 1 to 5 percent |
| Very unlikely | 5 to 20 percent |
| Unlikely | 20 to 45 percent |
| Roughly even chance | 45 to 55 percent |
| Likely | 55 to 80 percent |
| Very likely | 80 to 95 percent |
| Almost certain | 95 to 99 percent |

Confidence is stated as low, moderate, or high. Example: 'We assess it is likely that the domain is part of a targeted credential-phishing effort, with moderate confidence, because the evidence is consistent but comes from only two independent sources.' Never use 'could' or 'might' as a substitute, because readers hear anything from 5 to 95 percent.

**Source rating.** The Admiralty-style system rates the source's reliability (A completely reliable to F cannot be judged) separately from the information's credibility (1 confirmed to 6 cannot be judged). A well-known vendor (A) can pass on an unverified claim (4), and an anonymous forum poster (F) can post something you independently confirm (2). Count **circular reporting** once: five blogs repeating one tweet are one source.

**Biases to name and counter.** Confirmation bias (seeking facts that fit), anchoring (the first tool result frames everything), availability (the last incident you saw looks like this one), mirror imaging (assuming the adversary thinks like you), and attribution bias (jumping to a famous named actor). Countermeasures: ACH, a second analyst's review, writing the disconfirming evidence into the report, and refusing to name an actor without strong, independent links.

sections.heading: The OSINT report: structure and audience
sections.content:
A report is the product. If the reader cannot act on it or cannot tell what is known from what is guessed, the investigation had no value. A durable structure:

| Section | Contents | Common failure |
|---|---|---|
| Bottom line (BLUF) | One to three sentences: the assessment, confidence, and the decision needed | Buried at the end after pages of method |
| Objective and scope | The question asked, who requested it, time window, what was out of scope | Scope creep into unrelated people or systems |
| Methodology and sources | Tools and versions, passive or active, collection dates, source ratings | 'Open sources were used' with nothing specific |
| Findings with evidence | Numbered findings, each with its source, timestamp, and an evidence reference | Inference written as fact |
| Assessment and confidence | Competing hypotheses considered, estimative term, confidence level, key assumptions | Missing confidence, or 'might be' language |
| Limitations | What could not be seen, stale data, single-source items, gaps | Omitted, which hides risk |
| Recommendations | Concrete, prioritized actions with owners | Vague advice such as 'be vigilant' |
| Appendices | IOC table, graph export, evidence log, TLP marking | Missing expiry or context for IOCs |

**Write for the requester.** The same facts change shape depending on the reader. A SOC manager or incident responder wants the BLUF, the IOCs, and the immediate actions. An executive wants business impact, a decision, and a one-line confidence statement. A legal or privacy team wants data-handling detail and any personal data involved. A takedown or abuse desk wants exact URLs, timestamps, and evidence that satisfy the registrar's requirements. An external sharing partner wants a STIX bundle and a TLP marking. Write the report for the primary reader and put detail in appendices.

**Separate fact from judgment.** Use plain labels: 'Observed' for what you saw, 'Reported' for what a source claimed, 'Assessed' for your inference. Each assessed statement carries an estimative term and a confidence level.

**Defensible documentation.** A colleague, auditor, or court should be able to reproduce your work. Record for every item: the URL or query, the access time in UTC, the tool name and version, the module or settings, the analyst, and a preserved copy (screenshot plus archived page, with a hash of the file). Keep a running log as you work instead of reconstructing it afterward. Keep original evidence read-only and work from copies. Include a distribution marking such as TLP, and defang indicators in text (hxxp, [.]) so the report cannot be clicked into a live compromise.

**Pitfall: unsourced claims.** Any sentence the reader might challenge needs a reference. If you cannot cite it, either downgrade it to a lead or leave it out.

sections.heading: Legal, ethical, and OPSEC recap for the whole workflow
sections.content:
Every stage of the workflow, from collection to publication, carries obligations. The principles below apply from the first search to the final report.

| Principle | In practice | Failure example |
|---|---|---|
| Public-only | Use information that is genuinely accessible without bypassing access controls, fake credentials, or deception that violates terms | Logging in to a private forum with a borrowed account |
| Authorization | Only touch systems you own or are explicitly authorized to test; stay passive toward third parties | Port scanning an adversary's server |
| Minimization | Collect only what the objective requires; record bystanders' personal data only when essential; apply a retention period | Saving a whole family's social media for a domain case |
| Non-attributable research | Dedicated browser profile or virtual machine, separate egress, no personal or corporate-identity accounts, no contact with the adversary | Opening the phishing page from the analyst's own laptop on the corporate network |
| Evidence integrity | Capture originals, hash them, keep an immutable copy, log every handling step | Editing a screenshot or losing the original file |
| Safe handling | Treat all downloaded content as hostile; defang indicators; analyze in isolation | Clicking a live link from a report |
| Proportionality | Match the intrusiveness of the method to the severity of the question | A deep personal profile built for a low-risk spam message |

**Personas and attribution to people.** Naming a real individual is a different category of claim from naming a domain. Names can be stolen, photos reused, and profiles forged to frame someone. Do not publish or circulate an identity as the offender without strong, independent, corroborated evidence, and pass such findings to legal counsel or law enforcement instead of acting on them yourself. Doxxing an innocent person causes real harm and legal exposure.

**Sock-puppet and engagement policy.** Interacting with a threat actor through a created persona is an operation, not research. It needs written approval, a defined purpose, and legal review. It is outside the scope of routine OSINT.

**Data protection.** Personal data in leaked sets remains personal data. Apply the relevant privacy law (for example GDPR where it applies), restrict who sees the data, record why it was needed, and delete it when the case closes. Report to the affected account owners through the organization's normal process rather than redistributing the data.

**What is important to ask.** Am I authorized for this specific action? Is the method proportionate? Could this collection identify or harm someone who is not the target? Can I prove how the evidence was obtained and that it was not altered?

sections.heading: Worked example: a consolidated threat-intel report
sections.content:
Earlier OSINT steps produced three threads. A newly registered domain (acme-payrol1-portal[.]example) mimics a payroll portal. A persona claiming to be an HR contractor appeared on a professional network three weeks ago. A paste site entry holds 40 corporate email addresses. The analyst consolidates them with ACH and writes the report below.

**Title:** Suspected credential-phishing preparation against Acme staff. **TLP:** AMBER.

**1. Bottom line.** We assess it is likely (55 to 80 percent) that the lookalike domain and the HR-contractor persona are part of one targeted credential-phishing effort against Acme employees, with moderate confidence. Recommended decision: block the domain now and brief the 40 listed employees.

**2. Objective and scope.** Determine whether the domain, persona, and paste entry are related and whether they threaten Acme. Window: last 30 days. Out of scope: any contact with the persona or the site.

**3. Methodology.** Passive sources only: certificate transparency, passive DNS, RDAP, third-party URL-scan snapshot, search of the paste site. No direct visit. Collection on 2 November 2026 UTC; tool versions and queries are in the evidence log (Appendix B).

**4. Findings.**
- F1 (Observed, source rated B2): the domain was registered 6 days ago and a certificate was issued 5 days ago.
- F2 (Observed, B2): it resolves to 203.0.113.45, a shared host; the shared IP alone is not a link.
- F3 (Observed, C3): the snapshot shows a login form with Acme branding.
- F4 (Observed, C3): the persona profile names Acme as a client; its photo has a reverse-image match to a stock library, so the persona is likely fabricated.
- F5 (Observed, B2): the paste lists 40 acme.example addresses, no passwords, matching the public staff directory.

**5. Assessment.** H1 (targeted effort) fits F3, F4, and F5. H2 (commodity mass kit) conflicts with Acme-specific branding. H3 (internal simulation) conflicts with the absence of a simulation ticket. The link between persona and domain is weak: it rests on timing and the company name only. The paste is likely scraped from public sources, with moderate confidence.

**6. Limitations.** No registrant data (privacy service); single-source snapshot; persona and domain not linked by any unique attribute; no direct page analysis.

**7. Recommendations.** Block at DNS and proxy; search resolver and mail logs for the domain since its registration; brief the 40 employees and review their MFA; file an abuse report with the registrar; re-check persona links in 7 days.

| Type | Value (defanged) | Context | Confidence | Expiry |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Domain | acme-payrol1-portal[.]example | Lookalike login page | Moderate | 30 days |
| IP | 203.0.113.45 | Shared host, block only at the domain level | Low | 14 days |
| URL path | hxxps://acme-payrol1-portal[.]example/login | Credential form | Moderate | 30 days |
| Account | Persona profile, display name Jordan Vale | Probable fabricated persona; not a real-person attribution | Low | Review in 7 days |

Notice what the report does not do: it names no threat actor, avoids unsourced claims, and states which links are weak. That restraint is what makes it defensible.

quiz.question: A SOC analyst wants to see what an outsider could learn about the company's own domain (email addresses, subdomains, hosts) while leaving a minimal footprint. Which approach fits best?

options.label: Run a full active port and service scan of every host found, to confirm what is exposed
Run a harvester against passive sources such as search engines and certificate transparency logs
Build a Maltego graph of the CEO's personal social accounts and family members
Browse the OSINT Framework directory and treat the listed links as the finished result

quiz.explanation: A harvester pointed at passive sources shows the domain footprint an attacker could see, using third-party data and without touching the organization's systems more than necessary. A full active scan is intrusive and unneeded for this question. Profiling the CEO's family goes beyond the objective and breaks minimization. The OSINT Framework is a directory of where to look, not a collection of results.

quiz.question: A graph links twelve suspected phishing domains through one shared IP address. The IP belongs to a budget hosting provider with thousands of tenants. How should the analyst treat this link?

options.label: As strong proof that one operator runs all twelve domains, so attribution can be stated
As worthless, so the analyst should delete the IP from the investigation completely
As an IOC that should be blocked at the firewall for every customer of that host
As a weak edge, then pivot to stronger shared attributes such as registrant email or tracking ID

quiz.explanation: A shared IP on multi-tenant hosting is a weak relationship because unrelated sites live there, so it is a lead rather than proof. The right move is to look for unique shared attributes such as a non-privacy registrant email, an analytics ID, or an unusual certificate. Calling it strong proof overstates the evidence. Deleting it throws away useful context. Blocking the whole IP would likely cause false positives against legitimate sites.

quiz.question: You are asked to investigate a suspected live phishing site. What is the best first step to avoid tipping off the operator?

options.label: Query passive sources and a third-party snapshot of the page before any direct visit from your network
Open the URL from the corporate network so the full page behavior is recorded in the proxy logs
Submit test credentials to the login form to see whether the kit validates them
Run a DNS brute-force against the site's nameservers to discover all of its hidden subdomains

quiz.explanation: Passive collection and third-party snapshots reveal content and history without the operator seeing your address in their access logs, so they have no reason to rotate infrastructure. Visiting from the corporate network exposes a recognizable source. Submitting credentials interacts with the criminal system and may be unlawful. DNS brute-force is an active technique against the target's own infrastructure and is noisy.

quiz.question: In an Analysis of Competing Hypotheses matrix, one evidence item (a domain registered recently) is marked consistent with all three hypotheses. What does this tell the analyst?

options.label: It is the strongest evidence, because every hypothesis agrees with it
It should be given extra weight when the final confidence level is chosen
It has little diagnostic value, so attention should go to evidence that separates the hypotheses
It proves the first hypothesis in the list, since that one was written down earliest

quiz.explanation: Evidence that fits every hypothesis cannot help choose between them, so its diagnostic value is low. The useful items are those inconsistent with some hypotheses, which let the analyst eliminate explanations. Universal agreement is not strength, and it should not inflate confidence. Listing order has nothing to do with truth; assuming the first hypothesis is right is a form of anchoring.

quiz.question: Which opening best serves a SOC manager reading an OSINT report about a suspected phishing preparation?

options.label: A long methodology narrative covering every tool installed, with the conclusion left for the last page
A short bottom line: assessment with an estimative term, confidence level, and the decision requested
A list of all collected raw data with no interpretation, so the reader can reach conclusions alone
A statement that the activity might be malicious, with advice to stay vigilant and monitor the situation

quiz.explanation: A bottom line gives the manager the judgment, how sure the analyst is, and what action is wanted, with detail following in later sections. A methodology-first report buries the answer. Raw data without analysis shifts the analyst's job to the reader. Vague wording such as might and stay vigilant carries no probability, no confidence, and no actionable recommendation.
